newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Sievert-EMU needs no early political union.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Sievert-EMU needs no early political union.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Olaf Sievert said on Monday that the European Union's planned monetary union did not require big steps towards political integration right from the start.

The future European central bank would in fact find it easier to establish its independence if there were no political integration at first, Sievert said in the text of a speech on the advantages of the single currency.

"In Germany more than elsewhere it is assumed that a workable currency union requires big steps towards political union from the start," said Sievert, who is also president of the state central bank for Saxony and Thuringia.
"Here one probably exaggerates. What may well belong together in the very long term could initially prove to be disparate.

"The European central bank will at first need to spend years acquiring practical experience of its independence. It will find this easier if other political forces which might exert -- illegitimate -- influence remain largely decentralised for the time being."
The single currency, the Euro, is set to be introduced in 1999.
Sievert added that currency union would give rise to many unjustified demands for transfer payments which a political union might find it hard to limit.

"In a simultaneous political union it would be hard to keep such transfer demands limited to the levels likely to be set by the...only gradually increasing willingness of European nations to engage in pan-union solidarity," Sievert said.
A copy of the speech was made available ahead of delivery.
Sievert also said that currency union would enjoy good starting conditions if launched on time. Inflation across Europe was lower than expected and wage demands had been moderate in recent years.
